items.prompt: Marcus's facts about the checkout database were accurate, yet nothing was funded. What best explains that?
choices: Elena does not trust engineers on infrastructure topics
Facts describe a mechanism, not a cost or a date
The facts were too detailed for anyone to remember
items.explanation: Accuracy is not decidability: Elena received true statements and no cost, date or choice.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a technical risk?
choices: Failures during a sale could cost about $18,000 a minute
Customers may leave if checkout breaks
The connection pool is running at 62% utilization
items.explanation: A technical risk is a fact about system behavior in engineering terms; the other two describe business loss.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a business risk?
choices: Failure at peak means lost sales and visible customer complaints
Query plans regressed under heavy concurrent writes to the primary
The pool is currently at 62% of its connection limit
items.explanation: Business risk restates the fact as what the company stands to lose.

items.prompt: What does "keep an eye on it" usually signal from a business leader?
choices: She has informally approved the work to proceed
She heard a fact, not a decision to make
She has politely rejected the request outright
items.explanation: It is what leaders say when nothing actionable was put in front of them.

items.prompt: Elena weighs Marcus's request against a marketing campaign and a hiring plan. What did those asks arrive with that his did not?
choices: Endorsements from other executives
Detailed appendices explaining where each metric comes from
Dollars, dates and headcount she could compare
items.explanation: Competing asks come in units a budget owner already tracks; a pool percentage does not.

items.prompt: Would defining "connection pool" for Elena fix the problem?
choices: No, because she still has no cost or date to act on afterward
Yes, once she understands the mechanism it creates urgency
Yes, provided the definition uses a good analogy
items.explanation: Elena asked about last year's outage, not about vocabulary; the gap is the translation to cost and timing.

items.prompt: A technical risk is best described as
choices: A decision a leader made about priorities
A fact about system behavior under a condition
A forecast of the budget a team will request
items.explanation: It is engineer-native: a percentage, a vulnerability, a growth curve.

items.prompt: Translating technical risk into business risk changes what about the underlying fact?
choices: Whether the fact is true
How severe the underlying fact actually is under load
How it is expressed, not whether it is true
items.explanation: Translation keeps the fact and its severity intact and changes only the units it is stated in.

items.prompt: A platform engineer tells the head of product: "The nightly backup job has been failing silently for three weeks." She replies, "Thanks for flagging." Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: The head of product lacks the technical background to grasp what a backup job is there to protect
Three weeks of failures is too short a stretch for a backup problem to count as significant at all
The engineer should have labeled the issue critical so that its seriousness was obvious to her
The message names the failure but not what lost data would cost or when a restore would matter
items.explanation: Like Marcus, the engineer gave a true fact with no impact, no date and no choice, so "thanks" is the natural reply.
items.reference:
Same fact, two framings
technical: pool at 62%, query-plan regression
business: lost sales at peak, customers affected, by a date
the fact is identical; only the units change
Why: a leader decides on cost and timing, so a mechanism alone gives her nothing to act on.
items.learnMore:
Why accurate facts can still produce no decision

Engineers describe risk the way they experience it, mechanism first. A leader allocating budget compares asks in dollars, dates and headcount, so a fact without a cost and a date reads as a status update.

Common mistake

Assuming that if every sentence was true, the listener has what she needs. Truth is necessary for a decision, not sufficient.
items.reflection: Think of a time you gave someone accurate information and nothing happened. What did they still not have in order to act on it?

items.prompt: Which pairing translates a technical risk into business terms without changing the underlying fact?
choices: Pool at 62% becomes: 62% of customers will be unable to complete checkout during busy hours of the day
Pool at 62% becomes: the database is healthy today and needs no funding or attention at all this year
Pool at 62% becomes: at 8% monthly growth, checkout fails under normal load in about six months
Pool at 62% becomes: the platform will go down within days unless the whole system is rebuilt right away
items.explanation: Translation preserves the fact and adds cost or timing; the others invent a different fact, reassure, or inflate.

items.prompt: Elena used to be a database engineer and understands connection pools completely. Does the translation still matter?
choices: No, a technical listener can derive the cost and date of a failure without help from the engineer
Yes, because knowing the mechanism does not supply the cost, date, or options she must weigh
No, shared vocabulary closes the gap between engineer and leader completely once both understand it
Yes, but only because she may forward the message later to readers without a technical background
items.explanation: The gap was never vocabulary. Even an expert needs the dollars, the date and the options to decide.

items.prompt: Which set lists the parts of a decision-ready risk explanation?
choices: Mechanism, severity label, owner, and an apology
Root cause, stack trace, bug timeline, and a ticket link
Probability, impact, a by-when date, and options
items.explanation: Those four map the fact onto what a decision runs on.

items.prompt: In this framing, probability means
choices: How likely it is and how that changes over time
Whether the engineer feels confident about the analysis
The percentage of capacity currently in use
items.explanation: A single yes/no is not enough; the trend over time matters.

items.prompt: Impact is best expressed in
choices: Severity labels such as high or critical
Dollars or customers she tracks
Engineering hours spent building the fix
items.explanation: Severity labels are technical judgments; dollars and customers are comparable.

items.prompt: The exposure window is
choices: How long an outage lasts once it begins
The meeting slot reserved for raising the risk
When a risk stops being hypothetical
items.explanation: It is a date or event, not a feeling of urgency.

items.prompt: In a risk explanation, an option is
choices: A path with its own cost and the risk it removes from the picture
The engineer's single preferred fix, stated firmly
A list of every technical approach the team considered
items.explanation: An option is something a leader can choose or decline.

items.prompt: Which is a usable "by when"?
choices: This is getting urgent for the platform team
Checkout fails under normal load around week 27
Sometime soon, most likely, if nothing changes
items.explanation: A date is checkable against her calendar; urgency is not.

items.prompt: Why offer at least two options?
choices: So the engineer can hide a preferred answer in the list
So the meeting runs longer and looks thorough to attendees
So she faces a real trade-off rather than a bare verdict
items.explanation: One option is a verdict in disguise.

items.prompt: Which part tells the leader how much is lost if the risk happens?
choices: Impact
Probability
Exposure window
items.explanation: Probability says how likely and the window says when; impact says what it costs.

items.prompt: An engineer says: "If we do nothing, checkout fails under normal load around week 27, and at sale-level peak it fails today. A failed hour at peak costs roughly $1.1 million. I have three ways to address it." Which part is still missing?
choices: Option details: what each of the three ways costs and how much risk it removes
Impact: what a failure costs in units the leader already tracks, such as lost sales
Exposure window: the date or event when the risk stops being hypothetical
Probability: a sense that the failure is likely and getting closer over time
items.explanation: Impact, date and likelihood are all present; "three ways" without cost or risk removed gives the leader nothing to choose between.
items.reference:
What a decision-ready risk contains
probability: how likely, and how it changes
impact: cost in units the listener tracks
by when: the date the risk becomes real
options: costed paths with risk removed
Why: leaders decide by weighing cost against timing, and need alternatives to choose between.
items.learnMore:
The four parts of a decision-ready explanation

Probability says how likely and how that grows without action. Impact says what it costs in dollars or customers. The exposure window gives a date. Options give the leader something to choose between.

Common mistake

Giving impact in dollars but leaving timing as "urgent". A cost with no date still does not tell her whether to act this quarter.
items.reflection: Pick a risk you carry at work or in life. Could you state its likelihood, cost, deadline and two ways to respond?

items.prompt: Which statement gives impact in business units but leaves out the by-when?
choices: At current growth the pool crosses capacity around week 27, costing about $18,000 per minute of downtime
Failure is expected within six months, so the outage is rated critical severity
By the sale weekend we will be over the limit, and each minute down costs $18,000
A checkout failure during the sale would cost about $18,000 per minute, and it is quite likely
items.explanation: Only the first states a cost with no date; the second and fourth have both, and the third has a date but only a severity label.

items.prompt: A nightly backup failure has no growth curve to project. What is the honest by-when?
choices: A date chosen mainly because it sounds urgent, since leaders respond well to deadlines
No date at all, because an unknown date means that no exposure window exists
The next dated event that would make it real, such as the audit or release freeze
The date that the fix ticket was opened, since that is when the clock starts running
items.explanation: Without a trend, anchor on a real upcoming event the leader already tracks; inventing a date is catastrophizing and omitting one hides the risk.

items.prompt: Why is a pool percentage hard for Elena to weigh against a hiring plan?
choices: It is not in dollars, dates or headcount
Percentages are too imprecise to be compared across teams
She does not understand what a percentage represents
items.explanation: Comparison needs shared units; the percentage does not say what happens if it is ignored.

items.prompt: 62% utilization growing 8% a month reaches capacity in about
choices: Six weeks, because growth compounds quickly
Roughly six months, which lands around week 27
Two years, because 62% is still a comfortable margin
items.explanation: Compounding at 8% takes 62% to 100% in a little over six months.

items.prompt: At about 3x normal traffic, the 62% pool would be at roughly
choices: 93%, which is still within the limit
124%, which only just passes the limit
186%, already over capacity
items.explanation: 62% times 3 is 186%, so the sale peak is already beyond the limit.

items.prompt: Why is "around week 27" better than "urgent"?
choices: She can check the date against her own calendar
It sounds more technical and authoritative
It is harder to argue with because it is vague
items.explanation: A specific date is falsifiable and schedulable.

items.prompt: In the utilization chart, what does the 100% mark represent?
choices: The utilization the team should aim for
The projected point where the pool runs out
The average utilization across the whole year
items.explanation: It marks the date the risk stops being hypothetical.

items.prompt: A date claim being falsifiable means
choices: It cannot be tested against anything
Finance has already approved it
Later events can show it was wrong
items.explanation: Falsifiable claims are specific enough to be checked, which earns trust.

items.prompt: Elena asked whether this was like last year's outage. That question was
choices: An attempt to translate it into familiar terms
A sign that she had stopped listening to him
A request for a longer technical explanation of the cause
items.explanation: She was reaching for a business comparison; Marcus could have supplied it.

items.prompt: Which event makes a natural anchor for the checkout capacity risk?
choices: The engineer's next sprint planning meeting
A seasonal sale at about 3x normal traffic
The last edit to the pool configuration file
items.explanation: A known traffic event is a date the leader already plans around.

items.prompt: A reporting disk is 70% full, and usage grows 5% a month, compounding. Which claim is the dated version?
choices: The disk is at 70% and trending upward, which is getting concerning and is worth watching very closely
At this growth the disk fills in roughly seven months, so the purchase must be approved before then
Disk usage is high and growth is steady, so this should be handled soon by the storage team this year
At this growth the disk will not fill for about two years, so no purchase is needed for now at all
items.explanation: ln(100/70) over ln(1.05) is about 7.3 months. The vague options carry no date, and two years is wrong arithmetic.
items.reference:
Why a date beats "urgent"
62% x 1.08 per month reaches 100% in about 6 months (week 27)
at 3x sale traffic: 62% x 3 = 186%, already over
a date can be checked against a calendar
Why: a falsifiable date lets a leader weigh the risk against launches, peaks and budget cycles.
items.learnMore:
Dated claims are checkable claims

"Urgent" is a technical judgment a leader cannot verify. "Around week 27" can be set against her own calendar and shown wrong by events, which is what makes it useful and credible.

Common mistake

Treating a percentage as if it carried a timeline. 62% says where you are, not when you arrive at 100%.
items.reflection: What deadline in your own work is so familiar to others that attaching a risk to it would make it instantly clear?

items.prompt: The unit gives two answers for "by when": around week 27, and already today. Why?
choices: Normal traffic reaches the limit around week 27, while a 3x sale peak is already past it
One is an estimate and the other is the engineer's worst-case guess about that same level of load
Each date uses a different growth rate for what is really the same underlying traffic pattern
Week 27 refers to the pool and today refers to the separate query-plan regression issue

items.prompt: A marketing pause halves growth from 8% to 4% a month. What happens to the dated claim?
choices: It stays at week 27, because the pool's limit itself has not changed at all in the meantime
It shrinks to about three months, because slower growth somehow makes the situation more risky
It cannot be restated until the pause has ended and a new growth rate has actually been observed
It moves out to roughly 12 months and should be restated; the sale-peak exposure is unchanged

items.prompt: Catastrophizing means
choices: Describing every single risk in terms of dollars lost
Stating a risk as more severe than the evidence shows
Raising a risk with a leader before it is fully certain
items.explanation: The problem is the gap between claim and evidence, not the raising of it.

items.prompt: Minimizing means
choices: Leaving out all technical jargon from the explanation
Waiting for a second opinion before saying anything
Stating a risk as less severe than the evidence shows
items.explanation: Often done to avoid an uncomfortable conversation.

items.prompt: Which is a calibrated statement?
choices: At current growth, we cross capacity around week 27
This could take down the whole platform any day now
It's probably fine; we'll deal with it eventually
items.explanation: It states trend, date and nothing more or less.

items.prompt: What does a catastrophized warning cost over time?
choices: Leaders fund every future request immediately
Leaders start discounting later warnings from that source
Nothing at all, provided the risk was real
items.explanation: Once the gap shows, trust in future warnings drops.

items.prompt: What does minimizing cost the leader?
choices: She acts too quickly on a weak signal
She approves more budget than was necessary
She decides with too little information
items.explanation: She is under-informed for the decision she is actually making.

items.prompt: Does calibrated framing mean hedging every sentence?
choices: No, it means the numbers are the real ones
Yes, hedging protects the engineer's credibility
Yes, except when quoting dollar figures
items.explanation: Calibration is about accuracy of probability and impact, not vagueness.

items.prompt: Why not always present the worst case to secure funding?
choices: Worst cases are rarely plausible in any real system
Leaders start discounting every later warning
Finance rejects any figure labeled as a worst case
items.explanation: The short-term win costs long-term credibility.

items.prompt: A calibrated framing is trustworthy mainly because
choices: It is guaranteed to be funded
It avoids numbers that might turn out wrong
Her next warning can be believed in either direction
items.explanation: Credibility compounds across warnings.

items.prompt: A dependency's support ends in four months. Which statement is calibrated?
choices: Support is ending soon, so the platform may be compromised at any moment and we should act at once now
Support is ending, but it has worked for years so this is basically a non-issue for the team to track
Support ends in four months; after that, security fixes stop and any new flaw stays open until we migrate
Support may end at some point, and there could possibly be some exposure afterward for us to consider
items.explanation: The calibrated version states date and consequence. The others catastrophize, minimize, and hedge into mush.
items.reference:
Three framings of one fact
catastrophized: "could take down the platform any day"
minimized: "probably fine, we'll deal with it eventually"
calibrated: "at current growth we cross capacity around week 27"
Why: calibrated numbers keep the next warning believable in either direction.
items.learnMore:
Credibility is the asset

An inflated warning teaches the leader to discount the next one; a downplayed risk teaches her to over-react. Calibrated framing keeps both the numbers and your credibility intact.

Common mistake

Believing calibrated means hedged. It means the numbers are the real ones, not softened sentences.
items.reflection: Recall a colleague whose warnings you stopped taking seriously. Were they inflating, or had they been wrong the other way once?

items.prompt: What best shows a statement has been catastrophized rather than calibrated?
choices: It includes a dollar figure for the loss that is expected to follow
It claims certainty or scale that the measurements do not show
It names a specific date for when the risk becomes real to the company
It is delivered to the leader with a strong sense of urgency attached
items.explanation: Dollars, dates and urgency can all be calibrated; the test is the match to the evidence.

items.prompt: A team's earlier risk was minimized and an outage followed. What should its next warning do?
choices: Give the real numbers and say plainly what is still uncertain
Overstate the next risk to make up for last quarter's silence
Avoid numbers so nobody can say the team was wrong again
Wait until the risk is certain before saying anything at all
items.explanation: Overcorrecting to alarm or silence repeats the miscalibration. Credibility returns through accurate numbers and honest uncertainty.

items.prompt: A translated risk should end with
choices: A single firm recommendation from the engineer
A request that the leader investigate further herself
At least two options, each with a cost attached
items.explanation: Options turn a diagnosis into a decision.

items.prompt: Each option should state
choices: Its cost and how much risk it removes
Which engineer on the team prefers it
Which internal tools it would use
items.explanation: Cost and risk removed are the two things a leader trades.

items.prompt: Why is "this needs to be fixed" not enough?
choices: It is too polite to be persuasive
It leaves no choice to make
It lacks technical detail about the cause
items.explanation: It is a conclusion, not a choice.

items.prompt: Where does the recommendation belong?
choices: Instead of the options, to keep the meeting short
In a footnote added after the meeting ends
After the options, so the trade stays visible
items.explanation: Keeping it after preserves the visible trade-off.

items.prompt: A decision is a real trade-off when
choices: Paths differ in cost and risk removed
Every path costs exactly the same amount
Only a single path is put in front of her
items.explanation: Without differences, there is nothing to weigh.

items.prompt: Which is a costed option?
choices: Do something about the database fairly soon, before it becomes a larger problem
Read replica: 3–4 engineer-weeks, an estimated 6–12 months of runway
Consider scaling the system at some point in the coming year
items.explanation: A costed option names a price and a benefit.

items.prompt: A single verdict presented as the only path leaves the leader to
choices: Compare budgets with full confidence in the choice
Understand exactly what else could have been done
Approve or reject blindly
items.explanation: She cannot make a trade-off she cannot see.

items.prompt: Stopping at the diagnosis leaves the leader to
choices: Invent her own options
Verify all of the numbers herself
Escalate directly to the CEO
items.explanation: Without the technical background, she cannot cost alternatives.

items.prompt: Which package is decision-ready for an unpatched flaw in a login library?
choices: We must patch now, since delaying the release by two days is clearly worth it for the business as a whole.
Patching is the best option, and the firewall rule is far too risky for us to seriously consider as an alternative.
There are several ways to handle this flaw, so please tell me which of them you would prefer us to pursue.
Patch now: two engineer-days, closes the flaw, delays release two days. Firewall rule: half a day, blocks only the known path.
items.explanation: Two costed paths with risk removed let the leader trade. The others give a verdict, a strawman, or hand the work back.
items.reference:
Diagnosis, then options
diagnosis: probability, impact, by when
options: each with a cost and risk removed
recommendation: after the options, not instead of them
Why: a leader owns the trade-off between money, time and exposure, and needs the alternatives to make it.
items.learnMore:
Why a verdict is not a decision

"This needs to be fixed" hands back an unresolved statement. Two or more costed options make the decision a real trade-off the leader can own.

Common mistake

Presenting a single preferred fix as the only path, which leaves the leader approving or rejecting without understanding what else was possible.
items.reflection: Think of the last time you were handed one option. Would you have decided differently with a second one costed?

items.prompt: Which pair is two real options rather than one option and a strawman?
choices: Fix it properly right now at full cost versus simply leave it alone and ignore the risk forever
Build the replica now versus build the very same replica a quarter later at triple the cost involved
Read replica now (3–4 weeks, carries this sale) versus a config change (1 week, about 2 extra months)
Add one replica versus add a replica plus a second identical replica sitting right alongside the first
items.explanation: Real options are both credible and differ in cost and risk removed. Ignoring forever or a plainly worse twin makes the choice a foregone conclusion.

options: each with a cost and risk removed
recommendation: after the options, not instead of them

items.prompt: The COO says, "Just tell me what you would do." What is right?
choices: Refuse to answer, because the rule here is that you only ever present options
Give the recommendation, but restate the options and what each trades
Give the recommendation alone, since she asked for exactly that and nothing more
Name the cheapest option, since leaders in general tend to prefer the savings
items.explanation: She asked for a recommendation, which is fine after the options; dropping them hides the trade-off she owns.

items.prompt: Elena hears "62% utilization" as
choices: A number with no reference point to judge it against
A confirmed emergency needing action today
A formal request for additional budget
items.explanation: Nothing says whether 62% is fine or alarming.

items.prompt: "Query-plan regression" sounds to Elena like
choices: A funded project awaiting her sign-off
Engineering detail the team will handle
An executive-level decision to make now
items.explanation: Nothing signals that she needs to act.

items.prompt: Why does "we risk connection exhaustion" fail?
choices: It relies on far too many technical words
It exaggerates how serious the problem really is
No date, no size, nothing to compare
items.explanation: Hedged and open-ended, it cannot be scheduled or weighed.

items.prompt: Elena's question about last year's outage was
choices: An opening to answer in her own business terms
A signal that she wanted to end the topic
A request for a comparison between vendors
items.explanation: She was trying to translate it herself.

items.prompt: Marcus replied that it was "a capacity ceiling issue." That
choices: Fully answered her question about last year's outage
Stayed technical, handing translation back to her
Added a cost estimate to the technical explanation
items.explanation: The answer drew a technical distinction, not a business one.

items.prompt: That every statement was true shows
choices: Marcus misled her through what he left out
Elena simply was not paying close attention
Truth alone does not make a decision possible
items.explanation: Accurate facts can still leave the listener nothing to decide.

choices: No cost, date, or choice was ever stated

The meeting ran out of time before the end

items.prompt: What did none of the four statements supply?
choices: A definition of what a connection pool is
A cost and a date she could act on
An apology for introducing the regression

items.prompt: A DBA tells the head of sales: "Replication lag has crept to 9 seconds during business hours, which may be an issue for reporting." Which diagnosis mirrors Marcus's problem?
choices: A number with no reference point, plus a hedged "may be an issue" with no cost, date, or choice

The number was understated, so quoting a larger lag would have made the point land with her
The head of sales should have asked for a written technical document before the meeting began
items.explanation: Same pattern: a true figure and a hedge. Better vocabulary or a bigger number do not supply cost, date or choice.

items.prompt: The rewrite opens with
choices: A walkthrough of the mechanism behind connection pools
The ask and timeline, with a decision due this week
An apology for how the earlier explanation went
items.explanation: The reader should know immediately that a decision is needed.

items.prompt: At Black Friday-level traffic the pool is
choices: Fine until about week 27 in the worst case
Still within half of its total capacity
Already over its limit today at about 3x load
items.explanation: 62% times 3 is 186%.

items.prompt: Impact in the rewrite is expressed as
choices: About $18,000 in lost sales per peak minute
A critical severity rating on the ticket
A connection pool percentage and a trend line
items.explanation: Units Elena already tracks.

items.prompt: If Elena leaves after two paragraphs, she knows
choices: Only the technical cause of the problem and its history
A decision is due and peak exposure is real
Nothing that she could act on in the meeting
items.explanation: That is enough to fund the replica.

items.prompt: What does the rewrite recommend?
choices: Only the quick configuration change this week
Only the full sharding project, started right away
A read replica now, with sharding queued for next quarter
items.explanation: The replica covers the sale peak; sharding is the durable fix.

items.prompt: Why is sharding not the answer for this sale alone?
choices: It takes about a quarter, so it is too late for this year
It is the cheapest of the three options on offer
It does not reduce the capacity risk in any way
items.explanation: Durable but late.

items.prompt: Why put the nearer exposure first?
choices: Alarming facts should always come first
Her decision window is set by the sale
It is shorter to say aloud
items.explanation: Order by decision relevance.

items.prompt: The recommendation comes
choices: Before the problem is described
In place of the options themselves
After the options, not instead of them
items.explanation: It stays after so the trade-off remains visible.

items.prompt: A reporting database will pass capacity in about ten months at normal use, but a tax-filing rush in three weeks will push it past capacity. The budget decision is due next week. What leads?
choices: The ten-month trend, since it explains the mechanism and builds toward the rush
The three-week rush exposure, then the ten-month trend as context
The cost of each fix, since leaders care about money before anything else
Both facts side by side, so that neither one is privileged over the other
items.explanation: The rush sets the decision window; the trend is true but secondary.
items.reference:
Order of the rewrite
1. ask + timeline: decision this week
2. impact: about $18,000 per minute at peak
3. three costed options
4. recommendation, after the options
Why: a reader who stops early should already hold the facts that drive the decision.
items.learnMore:
Order by what a stopped reader needs

Put the fact that most affects the decision first, even if it is not the first thing you discovered. The nearer, more concrete exposure usually outweighs the slower trend.

Common mistake

Building up chronologically or technically and burying the fact that sets the decision window.
items.reflection: If your reader stopped after two paragraphs, would they have what they need to act?

The replica is simply the only one of the three options that costs less than the sharding project would
The configuration change cannot be carried out by this particular team in any case, whatever it costs
items.explanation: Compare options against the risk they remove by the relevant date.

items.prompt: The translation pattern generalizes to
choices: Only capacity risks and nothing else
Only risks that follow a steady growth rate
Most technical risks raised to a non-technical leader
items.explanation: The structure is general; the anchor varies.

items.prompt: Capacity risk anchors its by-when to
choices: A growth rate and a known event, like a sale
A CVE publication date and a patch release
A vendor contract renewal and its notice period
items.explanation: Growth projects forward; events mark exposure.

items.prompt: A disclosed vulnerability's timeline is driven by
choices: Monthly growth in traffic to the checkout service
How public the flaw is and whether a patch exists
Utilization of the primary database connection pool
items.explanation: Exposure grows as exploitation gets easier.

items.prompt: For an exploitable flaw, the dominant impact may be
choices: Lost sales from downtime of the checkout service
Engineer overtime paid during the incident response
Regulatory exposure or breach-notification costs
items.explanation: Impact units change with the risk.

items.prompt: As a flaw becomes more publicly documented, time to exploit
choices: Shrinks
Grows
Stays fixed regardless of exposure
items.explanation: More public means easier to exploit.

items.prompt: When the risk type changes, what happens to the pattern?
choices: Everything about the approach has to be replaced
The structure stays; anchor and impact units change
Nothing needs to change, including the timeline anchor
items.explanation: Probability, impact, by when and options still apply.

items.prompt: Why call the worked example "a case, not the whole territory"?
choices: It is a fictional story with invented figures
It is the only case where the method is valid
Other risks need different anchors and impact units
items.explanation: Learning the pattern means adapting it.

items.prompt: A natural by-when anchor for a compliance gap is
choices: The audit or regulatory deadline
The start date of the next sprint
The monthly growth rate of site traffic
items.explanation: Someone in the company already tracks that date.

items.prompt: An engineer reports that the admin console lacks audit logging, and an audit is nine weeks away. Which framing translates best?
choices: At current growth in admin usage we will be non-compliant in nine weeks, so we should plan our work accordingly.
Audit logging is missing from the admin console, and I would classify this as a high-severity gap for the company.
Auditors review in nine weeks; without logging we expect a finding that could delay certification. Here are two costed fixes.
Compliance gaps are urgent by their very nature, so we should fix this immediately before we do anything else.
items.explanation: The audit date is the anchor, and certification delay is the impact. A growth curve does not apply, and severity or urgency carry no date.
items.reference:
Same structure, different anchor
capacity: growth rate + a known event
vulnerability: how public the flaw is + patch status
compliance gap: the audit or regulatory deadline
always: probability, impact, by when, options
Why: the pattern generalizes, but each risk has its own real driver and impact units.
items.learnMore:
A worked case, not the whole territory

Marcus's example uses a growth curve and a traffic event as the anchor. Other risks have different drivers and different costs, but the translation still ends in probability, impact, a date and options.

Common mistake

Reusing the capacity framing on a risk whose timeline is not a growth trend.
items.reflection: Which risk in your own work would need a very different anchor than a growth curve?

items.prompt: Moving from the capacity case to an unpatched vulnerability, what changes and what stays?
choices: Everything changes, so the capacity case teaches nothing at all that would carry over to this new case
The anchor and impact units change; probability, impact, by when, and options stay
Only the dollar amounts change, while the timeline anchor remains a growth curve in every case
The options stay the same, but probability and the date are both dropped from the explanation
items.explanation: The structure is the transferable part; the real driver and cost units are case-specific.

items.prompt: No patch exists for a flaw, and the only option is to disable the feature. What is honest?
choices: Say what is known and unknown about exploit timing, and offer disabling versus accepting exposure, with costs
Wait until a patch exists, so that we avoid offering options that rest on assumptions nobody can support
Present disabling as the only path, because it is the only available fix and the leader needs clarity
Estimate a precise exploit date, so that the claim at least sounds fully dated even if it is a guess
items.explanation: A calibrated claim admits uncertainty yet stays decision-ready; inventing precision or withholding the choice both fail.
